findings.title: Delta encoding conflicts with the world server's existing drop-under-backpressure policy
findings.description: "Delta compression and state representation" says the client "reconstructs by accumulating deltas onto its last-known positions." But 300-arch ("Client connection lifecycle") already handles slow clients with "per-client send queues with backpressure-driven drops." Once a single delta frame is dropped, that client's positions are wrong for good, and nothing in the design corrects them. Quantization error also builds up when deltas are taken against the server's float positions instead of the client's quantized reconstruction. Decoupling the stream rate to 30 Hz makes this worse: deltas have to be taken between streamed frames, not between sim ticks, and the document doesn't say which. The design needs four things: deltas measured against a per-client acknowledged or quantized baseline, periodic keyframes, a resync path when a frame is dropped, and a rule that agents entering the frustum (Tier 3) get absolute positions. That last one means per-client baseline state, which is a real cost at about 50k visible agents per client. The world-wrap topology in the journal (`wide.yaml` uses an 800×400 wrap world) also turns every edge crossing into a "large delta" event, and that isn't mentioned either.

findings.title: Compression math and current wire format are both wrong
findings.description: "Current State" calls the wire "uncompressed JSON over WebSocket" and sizes it at "24 bytes × 3,500 agents". 24 bytes per agent is raw binary math, not JSON. 300-arch ("State representation and serialization") also specifies raw float buffers with a message-type-byte framing protocol. So either the document is wrong about the current format, or the implementation has drifted from 300-arch. Either way, Tier 2's "Binary WebSocket replaces JSON" may be work that's already done. Separately, "int16 … gives ~32× compression over float32 positions" is wrong. int16 against float32 is 2× per component. Against the stated 24-byte record it's 4× (int16 xyz = 6 bytes), and only if velocity is dropped from the wire. The Tier 3/4 bandwidth claims ("fits within 10G LAN or modern WiFi") rest on this number, so they need to be redone.

findings.title: The tick return contract is called the central decision but is left open, and two of its options break the stated invariant
findings.description: The overview says this document "defines the shared boundary — the tick return type contract". In fact it lists options (a)/(b)/(c) and says "support all three behind an abstraction, with the choice made per-platform." Option (b) is described as one that "leaks the compute substrate into the server", which directly contradicts the design goal "the world server should not need to know whether forces are computed by NumPy or Quadrants." "Envisioned State" also promises `tick() → state arrays` "preserved at every tick." Building all three is over-engineering. Recommendation: pick (a) now. It's nearly free on unified memory and correct everywhere. Name the measurement that would justify (c) on CUDA, and drop (b).

findings.title: GPU-resident state and neighbor caching contradict the stateless-engine contract in 100-arch
findings.description:
100-arch ("Envisioned State") says the engine is "stateless between ticks — all state lives in the arrays passed to it, including the spatial index. The caller (world server) owns the spatial index." Slice 119 (cached neighbor lists) and Tier 2's "full tick on GPU" both bring in persistent engine-side state: a neighbor cache, plus Quadrants fields that live across ticks. "Related Work" says this initiative "optimizes but does not change" 100-arch, but it does change it. Questions the document leaves open:
- Who owns the neighbor cache and the GPU-resident arrays?
- How do the world server's entity spawn and removal (300-arch: the server "allocates space in the state arrays") reach GPU memory?
- What happens to the cache when indices shift on removal?

The 100-arch contract has to be revised explicitly, or the design has to keep the cache in caller-owned arrays.

findings.title: "The wire is a separate problem" stops holding at Tier 3+
findings.description: At 250k–2M agents, server-side frustum culling and per-client delta encoding are O(N) per tick per client. If they run on CPU in NumPy, every tick needs the full position array off the GPU, which is the PCIe cost option (a) was meant to avoid at Tier 4. Doing culling and encoding efficiently at that scale means running them as GPU kernels next to the data. That couples the world server's wire pipeline to the compute substrate, against both the principle and the "Clean ownership boundaries" goal. Tier 4's "server-side render path (Vulkan framebuffer → H.264)" goes further and adds a renderer to the server. The document should say where culling and encoding run at each tier and which side owns them.

findings.title: The executor and threading contract isn't checked against Quadrants
findings.description: 300-arch requires `sim.step` to run on `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)`, and its parallelism with the asyncio loop depends on the compute releasing the GIL. The document doesn't check whether Quadrants/Taichi kernel launches and `to_numpy()` syncs release the GIL. It also doesn't check whether runtime init (`ti.init` or its Quadrants equivalent) and Metal command queues are tied to the thread that initialized them. If launches hold the GIL, Tier 2 brings back the slice-315 failure mode where WebSocket sends stall. 300-arch's planned move to a separate sim process with shared-memory IPC also rules out option (c), because DLPack handles don't cross processes. The "Quadrants substrate evaluation" slice should cover all of this explicitly.

findings.title: GPU spatial hash doesn't match the existing kNN (k=13) semantics, and that's where the difficulty is
findings.description: The current backend is `cKDTree.query k=13` (a topological cap). "Spatial query strategy shift" describes a radius gather ("gather neighbors from adjacent cells"). Getting top-k from a variable-size candidate set per agent on GPU takes per-thread partial selection or padded buffers, plus a prefix-sum pass to build the CSR. None of that is mentioned, and Entry 6 of the journal shows the same top-k step (`query_knn_batch`) on HashGrid wiped out its own gains in NumPy. The spatial hash will also return different neighbor sets and orders from the KD-tree, so "Same code, different backend" and "verifiable against the current NumPy implementation" can't mean bitwise equality.

findings.title: There are no measurable fidelity or determinism criteria, and GPU atomics break the determinism claim
findings.description: "Preserve behavioral fidelity" makes regression testing "mandatory" but doesn't say what passing means. Float32 GPU against float64 NumPy (100-arch mentions float64 sim precision) in a chaotic flocking system will diverge within a few ticks. The document needs a definition: either per-tick force tolerance on frozen inputs, or statistical metrics over trajectories. "Determinism within a given stagger configuration should still hold" won't be true on GPU if force accumulation uses float atomics, because summation order isn't deterministic. 300-arch's replay logging ("given a log and the same configuration, the simulation can be reconstructed tick-by-tick") depends on determinism. The document should say whether GPU tiers give up replay or require deterministic reduction.

findings.title: Multi-resolution and subset-evaluable tick are ignored in the GPU port
findings.description: 100-arch makes the subset-evaluable tick and heterogeneous (aggregate) neighbor types first-class interface requirements. It names them as the way to scale past tens of thousands of agents. This document goes to 2M on brute-force GPU throughput and never says whether the Quadrants kernels support an active-agent mask or aggregate neighbors. If the ported `BulkForce` kernels assume a dense full population, adding those features later means rewriting the kernels.

findings.title: Scope includes work that is out of scope or has no slices behind it
findings.description:
- "Biome terrain shading is viewer-only" is described as independent of all scaling work, while Scope excludes "viewer/client rendering optimization". Move it to a viewer initiative.
- Tiers 4–5 (25G LAN, Vulkan→H.264 server render path, two 1M populations) have no anticipated slices and no owner. They are vision, not architecture. Mark them explicitly as future work, outside this initiative's deliverables, so nobody designs the contract around them now.
- Supporting all three tick-return options is covered above. Cut it to one.

findings.title: The Current State budget doesn't match the headline number
findings.description: The phase budget comes from an N=2492 synthetic bench and adds up to about 9.4 ms (about 106 TPS). The headline is 57 TPS at N=3,500. Mixing these sources hides how much of the live tick is overhead outside the five phases (I/O, serialization, the executor hop). That overhead is exactly what the "profile before you optimize" principle would need as a baseline.

findings.title: The Quadrants API namespace is unverified
findings.description: The document writes `@ti.kernel (Quadrants)`. Since Quadrants is a fork, check its real module and decorator names before slice designs copy this. If the decorator doesn't exist under that name, the snippets won't import.
